clue.text: Reverberations in a dictionary of music by 27?

definitions.text: Reverberations in a dictionary of music by 27?

parts.words: Reverberations in a dictionary of music by 27?
parts.note: reverberations are echoes, Grove is the famous dictionary of music, and 27 points to Rosamond Lehmann, whose novel this is

explanation.surface: Someone looks up echoes in a music reference book compiled by the solver's 27-across.
explanation.walkthrough: Grove's Dictionary of Music and Musicians is the standard music reference, so echoes 'in Grove' describe the title of Rosamond Lehmann's 1953 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue describes the title of a Lehmann novel through its parts: resounding noise inside a book called Grove.

clue.text: Ruler frustrated in Hades, nevertheless a protector of spirits

definitions.meaning: the mythical king punished in the underworld with food and water always just out of reach
a locking stand that keeps decanters of whisky or brandy visible but out of reach

explanation.surface: A tormented king of the underworld turns out to guard the drinks cabinet.
explanation.walkthrough: The decanter stand is named after the mythical king because the bottles are seen but cannot be taken without the key.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek myth names the king tormented by unreachable fruit, and the household item is a lockable decanter stand named after him.

clue.text: Alienist's text is possibly suggesting French philosophers

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the preceding words may be arranged another way

parts.note: the possessive is read as plain letters, the S included

explanation.surface: A psychiatrist's writing seems to point towards Sartre and his circle.
explanation.walkthrough: An alienist is an old word for a psychiatrist. Here the S of 'Alienist's' counts as a letter, giving fifteen letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Sartre, de Beauvoir and Camus are the best-known members of this mid-century French school of thought.

clue.text: Pure content of Purchas' ten books based on Hakluyt

indicators.note: the content of a phrase is the letters running inside it, so the answer sits within the words

parts.words: Purchas' ten books based on Hakluyt

explanation.surface: Samuel Purchas's travel collection drew on Hakluyt's earlier voyages.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'PurCHAS' TEn'. Purchas his Pilgrimes was a continuation of Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste and pure are synonyms meaning untouched or virtuous.

clue.text: Till clown shows two types of bird with broken leg These writers have a point

parts.note: owls are one kind of bird
pie is an old name for the magpie

indicators.note: broken means the letters of leg are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: A clown displays a pair of birds, one with an injured leg.
explanation.walkthrough: Till Eulenspiegel, the German trickster, appears as Owlspiegle in Scott's The Abbot. The pie is the magpie. The words after 'leg' in this file are the next clue's, joined by OCR.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Scott's anglicised name for Till Eulenspiegel, the jester of German folk tales.

clue.text: These writers have a point

parts.note: the writers are not authors but pen tips, which are pointed

explanation.surface: Some authors make a valid argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Pen tips do the writing and each is sharpened to a point.

clue.text: Usher in a famous history

parts.note: the famous history is Shakespeare's Henry VIII, titled The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eighth, and the usher is a character in it

explanation.surface: Someone launches a celebrated historical era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Usher in' looks like a verb meaning to inaugurate; it is a noun, gentleman usher to Queen Katharine in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: In Henry VIII this character serves as gentleman usher to Queen Katharine and reports Wolsey's death.

clue.text: A candid consular version of Australian gamblers

indicators.note: a version of the words is a new arrangement of their letters

explanation.surface: An honest consul's account of gambling Australians.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Carey's Booker-winning novel is about two compulsive gamblers in nineteenth-century Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's two title characters are obsessive gamblers who bet on carrying a glass church across New South Wales.

clue.text: Waugh diarist?

explanation.surface: Was the novelist Waugh a keeper of diaries?
explanation.walkthrough: One name serves as Waugh's first name and as the surname of the Restoration diarist John.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist was christened with this name, and the Restoration diary-keeper who rivalled Pepys bore it as a surname.

clue.text: Novelist gives point to first-class letter-writer

parts.note: N, north, is a compass point
A1 is first-class, written AI
the apostle Paul wrote the epistles, letters of the New Testament

explanation.surface: An author gives a sharp edge to an excellent correspondent.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trinidad-born Nobel laureate V. S. Naipaul.
explanation.definitionFit: V. S. Naipaul wrote A House for Mr Biswas and won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

clue.text: Recommended French diet, 1789

parts.note: refers to Marie Antoinette's legendary advice to starving Parisians at the Revolution, 'let them eat cake'

explanation.surface: A nutrition guide issued in revolutionary France.
explanation.walkthrough: The French form of the saying is 'qu'ils mangent de la brioche'.
explanation.definitionFit: The rich bread is what the queen supposedly told the hungry poor to eat instead of bread.

clue.text: Sort of car used to make a true impress of an original?

definitions.meaning: read as two words, a kind of automobile

definitions.text: used to make a true impress of an original?
definitions.meaning: a photographic process for reproducing pictures in facsimile

explanation.surface: A model of motor car that copies things exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: An auto is a car so a car model is an auto type, and the carbon printing process made faithful facsimiles of artworks.

clue.text: "So swept the tumult and —, / Along the margin of Achray" (Scott)

definitions.text: "So swept the tumult and —, / Along the margin of Achray" (Scott)

parts.words: "So swept the tumult and —, / Along the margin of Achray" (Scott)
parts.note: the missing word from The Lady of the Lake, rhyming with Achray and meaning a brawl

explanation.surface: A line of Scott's verse with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Loch Achray is in the Trossachs, the setting of Scott's The Lady of the Lake; the gap must rhyme with it.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means a noisy fight in a public place, matching the tumult of the line.

clue.text: Early pumpkins blew on its coast

definitions.text: Early pumpkins blew on its coast

parts.words: Early pumpkins blew on its coast
parts.note: recalls Edward Lear's The Courtship of the Yonghy-Bonghy-Bo, set 'on the coast' where 'the early pumpkins blow'

explanation.surface: Squash plants flowered early along a seashore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' here means bloom, as in Lear's nonsense poem, not a gust of wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear names this stretch of south-east Indian shoreline as the place where the pumpkins blow.

clue.text: Deserves, say, Sir Thomas Browne subject matter

indicators.note: say signals that the word is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: one who deserves a reward earns it

explanation.surface: Sir Thomas Browne's material is worthy of praise.
explanation.walkthrough: Browne's Hydriotaphia, or Urne-Buriall, is about funeral vessels found in Norfolk. EARNS and URNS sound alike in British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Browne's treatise discusses ancient burial vessels holding ashes of the dead.

clue.text: "And when they're moulting, / They're pretty" (Ogden Nash)

definitions.text: "And when they're moulting, / They're pretty" (Ogden Nash)

parts.words: "And when they're moulting, / They're pretty" (Ogden Nash)
parts.note: the closing word of Nash's couplet, rhyming with moulting and meaning disgusting

explanation.surface: A quotation from a comic poem with its punchline missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme with 'moulting' and the sense of 'pretty' as 'quite' point to the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means disgusting, rounding off Nash's verse about moulting creatures.

clue.text: Donne's poem had metre revised

indicators.note: something revised is reworked, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: John Donne's verse had its rhythm rewritten.
explanation.walkthrough: A love poem in Donne's Songs and Sonnets.
explanation.definitionFit: Donne's lyric opens 'Dear love, for nothing less than thee / Would I have broke this happy' sleep.

clue.text: Its Abbot supervised revels north of the Border

definitions.text: Its Abbot supervised revels north of the Border

parts.words: Its Abbot supervised revels north of the Border
parts.note: the Scottish name for the Lord of Misrule, who led Christmas revelry

explanation.surface: A monastery head oversaw parties in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland the master of festive revels was called the Abbot of this, a title Scott used in The Abbot.
explanation.definitionFit: The festive title made the merrymaking head an abbot of folly and misrule, the opposite of sense.

clue.text: His contribution was abstract, and he was hung for it

definitions.text: His contribution was abstract, and he was hung for it

parts.words: His contribution was abstract, and he was hung for it
parts.note: an abstract painter whose works were hung in galleries, not a man hanged for a crime

explanation.surface: A man's offence was vague and he went to the gallows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hung' is used of paintings on gallery walls. Ben Nicholson is the leading British abstract painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Nicholson made white relief and abstract paintings that were exhibited in major galleries.

clue.text: Stevenson sailor from final anthology

indicators.note: the answer is taken from within the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A seafaring character of Stevenson's comes from the last collection.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Breck Stewart of Kidnapped; the letters run across 'finAL ANthology'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Breck is the Jacobite adventurer in Kidnapped, rescued at sea from a sinking boat.

clue.text: West Indian writer in Clarendon Press tome, revised

indicators.note: the writer's name lies in the run of letters through the words that follow

explanation.surface: An Oxford University Press volume on a Caribbean author has been revised.
explanation.walkthrough: Garth St Omer of St Lucia; the letters run across 'presS TOME Revised'. 'revised' looks like an anagram signal but only supplies its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Garth St Omer is a novelist from St Lucia in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Lively subject, and in time

parts.note: Penelope Lively wrote the novel A ... in Time, so the subject of her title plus 'in time' completes it

explanation.surface: An animated topic arrives punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: Lively is the novelist Penelope Lively, not an adjective; her children's novel is A Stitch in Time.
explanation.definitionFit: The title word of Penelope Lively's novel, from the proverb about sewing early saving nine.

clue.text: Steel town with permanent exhibition of Cretan art

definitions.meaning: a Spanish city famous for its swords and blades

definitions.text: with permanent exhibition of Cretan art
definitions.meaning: the Cretan is El Greco, who settled in this city and whose paintings are kept there

explanation.surface: An industrial city hosts a lasting display of Greek island art.
explanation.walkthrough: El Greco, 'the Greek', was born in Crete and worked in this Spanish city for most of his life.
explanation.definitionFit: The Castilian city was famed for fine sword blades and holds many works by the Crete-born El Greco.

clue.text: Chap's tie might be a mixture of styles

indicators.note: might be suggests the letters could form something else when rearranged

parts.note: the possessive is read as plain letters

explanation.surface: A man's necktie could be a clash of patterns.
explanation.definitionFit: A work imitating or blending several artistic manners is this, a borrowed medley.

clue.text: English study of London hero

parts.note: a den is a private room for reading or work

explanation.surface: An English research piece about a heroic Londoner.
explanation.walkthrough: London is Jack London; Martin Eden is the title hero of his novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Eden is the sailor-turned-writer at the centre of Jack London's novel.

clue.text: Her niece went to Rochester

parts.note: Rochester is not the Kent city but Jane Eyre's employer and husband; the niece is Jane, raised by her cruel aunt

explanation.surface: A woman's niece travelled to a city in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: In Jane Eyre the orphan is brought up at Gateshead by her aunt before going to Lowood and then to Mr Rochester.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Eyre's widowed aunt by marriage at Gateshead Hall raised her harshly.

clue.text: Old Greek intervals

parts.note: in ancient Greek music theory, an interval of two whole tones, a major third

explanation.surface: Breaks in ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek theorists named the major third after its two whole steps.

clue.text: She issued an invitation to the waltz

definitions.text: She issued an invitation to the waltz

parts.words: She issued an invitation to the waltz
parts.note: the woman is the novelist who published Invitation to the Waltz in 1932

explanation.surface: A hostess asked someone to dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Invitation to the Waltz is the novel's title, so 'issued' means published.
explanation.definitionFit: The English novelist published Invitation to the Waltz and its sequel The Weather in the Streets.
